record_reviews.summary: Waterhouse answers a prior Darwin letter after examining a nest and first recounts his direct observation of Osmia atricapilla excavating a circular mud cavity, smoothing its inside, and adding a lid (P1–3). He then theorises that the bee's fixed position determines cavity diameter and that successive curves close the cell until it must begin again (P4–6). The unfinished ending and absence of Darwin's preceding question prevent a direct pair here.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From George Robert Waterhouse 10 February 1858British MuseumFeb. 10. 58

record_reviews.summary: Waterhouse compares four wasp/wasp-relative nests: a ten-cell hexagonal nest, cylindrical Mischocyttarius cells, an irregular nest, and an Icaria comb whose cells become angular where they contact neighbours (P1–4). He contrasts wasp single-female construction with hive-bee construction and defends his cylinders-to-hexagons theory against Owen, including a question about packing circles and six neighbours (P5–8). Five accompanying sketches are separate visual enclosures; no Darwin prompt survives in this packet.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From G. R. Waterhouse 13 February 1858British MuseumFeb. 13. 58

record_reviews.summary: Waterhouse reports on notes he was asked to supply after the Entomological Society discussion of bee cells, explaining that he shortened them to the theoretical point and correcting the scope of 'accidental' (P1). He argues that wasp cells become hexagonal as new cells are added in the interstices and qualifies the outermost-row exception (P2–4), with a separately attached Icaria enclosure whose completeness is editorially uncertain. The actual Darwin note that 'bothers' him is absent.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From G. R. Waterhouse 17 April 1858British MuseumApril 17. 1858

record_reviews.summary: Waterhouse points Darwin to his printed observations on bee cells, reports Tegetmeier's experiments and Gray's and Smith's disagreement about lateral pressure, and asks Darwin for his view of Brougham's French Academy paper (P1–2). He separately recounts a German fossil-collection trip (P3–5) and asks about Tegetmeier's uncompleted wax-and-pegs experiment in the postscript (P6). The Zoologist report and prior Darwin prompt are cited apparatus, not a missing body reconstructed here.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From G. R. Waterhouse 2 August 1858British MuseumAugust 2d. 1858

record_reviews.summary: Darwin insists he checked every page of Waterhouse's parcel and that text is physically missing, while ruling out mislaying the map bundle (P1). He hopes Waterhouse can obtain another copy and responds humorously to the possibility of very ancient mammals (P2–3), then recalls Waterhouse's explanation of a rodent-free province and plans future questions (P5–6). The missing-page dispute and mammal remarks are distinct; Waterhouse's incoming 1642 does not answer the parcel question in its surviving text.
record_reviews.date_assessment: To G. R. Waterhouse 4 March [1855]Down Farnborough KentMarch 4th.—

record_reviews.summary: Waterhouse's 7 March source begins mid-sentence with a promised dispatch, then gives a detailed comparison of Ichthyosaurus and cetacean skulls: superficial resemblance contrasts with different type characters, including intermaxillaries versus maxillaries (P1–3). Its 2pp-incomplete metadata and opening fragment mean the antecedent is unavailable; CD's marginal '11' is separate provenance.

Darwin asks Waterhouse for an accessible systematic guide to British Lepidoptera for his sons, comparing Stephens, Westwood, and Humphreys and objecting to diffuse descriptions without family synopses (P1–5). This is a clear outgoing request, but no Waterhouse answer is preserved in the packet; the books named in footnotes are bibliographic context, not an incoming response.

record_reviews.summary: Waterhouse reports that the books Darwin named contain no bee-cell construction account, though one promises a future Osmia account (P1). He then describes the oval mud cell, smooth inner wall and rough outer surface, and recounts Entomological Society discussion of hive-bee cells, including Tegetmeier's exhibit (P3–4). The attached diagram is a separate visual; this April 1857 incoming source answers an earlier Darwin bee-cell inquiry not represented by an outgoing endpoint in this packet.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From George Robert Waterhouse 14 April 1857British MuseumApril 14. 57
